bib.title: Accelerating Scientific Discovery with Autonomous Goal-evolving Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Accelerating Scientific Discovery with Autonomous Goal-evolving Agents" (SAGA), Yuanqi Du (first author, equal-contribution group) et al., arXiv 2512.21782v2 [cs.AI], preprint, first posted Dec 2025 (v2 dated 30 Mar 2026). Code: github.com/btyu/SAGA (MIT).
COVERAGE: 272,629 chars / 114 pages extracted. Read in full: abstract, results 2.1-2.5, discussion, methods, S1 (framework, workflow, LLM setup, extensibility), S2.3 antibiotic ablations, nanobody workflows. Skimmed or skipped: remaining supplement S2-S7 (prompts, per-task figures, agent transcripts) and references (about 55 percent of the text, by grep only). The headline numbers below are all from the main text, which I read completely.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. SAGA is a bi-level loop. An outer loop of Planner, Implementer, Optimizer and Analyzer evolves the objectives. An inner loop optimizes candidates against the current objectives.
 number: none
 setup: Applied to 5 domains (antibiotics, nanobodies, DNA enhancers, inorganic materials, chemical process flowsheets).
 quote: "an outer loop of LLM agents analyzes optimization outcomes, proposes new objectives, and converts them into computable scoring functions, while an inner loop performs solution optimization under the current objectives" (abstract, p1)
2. Three autonomy levels, defined by which stages a human touches. This is the rung structure for note 07.
 number: 3 modes
 setup: Same prompt and initial objectives across modes. Methods 4.1.3, p18-19.
 quote: "Co-pilot: Human scientists collaborate closely with both the planner and analyzer... Semi-pilot: Human intervention is limited to the analyzer stage... Autopilot: All four modules operate fully autonomously without human intervention." Also: "strategic decisions about continuation, termination, or pivoting remain human-guided" (semi-pilot). Autopilot is for when "domain constraints are well-specified and trust in the system is established."
3. In the loops tested, the three modes perform about alike. Autopilot is often comparable to human-guided modes. The antibiotic task is the cleanest case: modes converge on the same objective types.
 number: none (qualitative)
 setup: Antibiotic task. Objectives after iteration 1 added little (S2.3.1, p48-49). Materials and DNA tasks: autopilot "comparable".
 quote: "SAGA autopilot achieves overall performance comparable to that obtained with human collaboration with respect to HepG2 specificity and even demonstrates improvements in sequence diversity and stability." Also: "the performance of the three different modes was relatively similar... objectives proposed by different modes in each iteration are convergent to a specific list of types."
4. Chemical process design is the exception. Less human input gives more variance.
 number: none
 setup: Butanol/water separation, RL inner loop, 3 iterations, p16.
 quote: "we see larger variation in individual objectives with less human intervention, particularly, for material flow intensity at semi- and autopilot level"
5. Dynamic objectives beat fixed objectives. SAGA-Opt is the optimizer alone, a fixed-objective baseline. It over-optimizes the primary objective (antibiotics: low drug-likeness; magnets: poor stability and Curie temperature). This is reward hacking by the optimizer.
 number: none
 setup: Antibiotic, materials, DNA tasks, vs SAGA-Opt, TextGrad, MolT5, NatureLM, AlphaEvolve, regLM, Biomni.
 quote: "optimization algorithms exploit gaps between models and reality, producing solutions that maximize predicted scores while missing important practical considerations" (p3); "SAGA-Opt... over-optimizes the primary biological objectives" (p4)
6. Nanobody PD-L1: 2-5x fewer oracle calls than the baselines.
 number: 2-5x
 setup: Compared with Germinal and BoltzGen, top 15 sequences each, AlphaFold3 + Boltz2 averaged.
 quote: "SAGA achieves this performance with 2-5 times fewer number of oracle calls than Germinal and BoltzGen."
7. Wet-lab nanobody result: 3 binders from 24 tested. The evolved composite score separates binders from non-binders where no single metric does.
 number: 3/24; KD 300-400 nM; p=0.03
 setup: BLI, PD-L1. Single metrics all p>0.05 (Mann-Whitney U).
 quote: "We identified three true binders, with a lowest dissociation constant (KD) of 300 nM"; "no single metric alone achieved statistical significance (all p>0.05; Mann–Whitney U test), yet the composite scoring function autonomously constructed by SAGA yielded a p-value of 0.03" (p8)
8. Wet-lab antibiotic result: 28 compounds tested; 4 with over 80% inhibition.
 number: 28 synthesized; 4 hits (compounds 4, 8, 9, 27); compound 8 Tanimoto 0.28
 setup: E. coli, 128 µg/mL, with polymyxin B nonapeptide (permeabilizer). Only compound 8 had minimal cytotoxicity in HEK293 and HepG2 at its MIC. The potency of compound 8 "needs to be further improved."
 quote: "compound 4, 8, 9, and 27 show more than 80% inhibition of bacterial growth at a concentration of 128 µg/mL when combined with PMB"; "Tanimoto similarity to all known antibiotics is only 0.28, less than the 0.4 threshold" (p5)
9. DNA enhancers: gains over baselines.
 number: 19.2-176.2% overall; MPRA specificity at least 48.0%; motif enrichment at least 47.9%; stability at least 1.7%; 88.8% of proposed objectives were statistically driven.
 setup: HepG2-specific enhancers, multiple independent runs, held-out metrics.
 quote: "surpass all baselines on metrics probing both statistical validity and biological function by 19.2-176.2% across multiple independent runs" (p9)
10. Materials: DFT/MLIP-validated outputs and a specific guardrail pattern. The agent adds thresholds so one objective is not over-optimized.
 number: more than 90% of crystals contain B/C/N/O; over 75% are transition-metal carbides/nitrides/borides; thresholds HHI<1500, Ehull<0.1 eV/atom
 setup: Superhard materials and rare-earth-free magnets.
 quote: "SAGA imposes reasonable thresholds on certain objectives, such as HHI score below 1500 and Ehull below 0.1 eV/atom... thereby preventing over-optimization of any single objective at the expense of overall performance" (p13)
11. Design pattern. The Implementer reports uncomputable objectives back to the Planner (retry loop). The Analyzer can end the run early, so termination is a decision of the loop. A selector picks from all iterations, not just the last.
 number: none
 setup: S1.2, p37-38.
 quote: "If the implementer determines that an objective is not computable in a reliable and feasible manner... it notifies the planner to revise the plan accordingly." Also: "The analyzer also determines whether candidates satisfy the goal and can trigger early termination when success criteria are met."

LIMITS (authors, p17)
- Needs computationally verifiable objectives: "SAGA currently relies on computationally verifiable objectives." Otherwise it needs human or lab-in-the-loop feedback.
- Design space is predefined by the goal (for example small molecules). It does not pick the modality.
- Not shown: no cost or token accounting for the LLM agents (the 2-5x saving counts oracle calls only), no ablation of the autonomy level that is statistically powered, no LLM-backbone ablation. Most evaluation is computational and uses held-out in-silico metrics. Wet-lab hit rates are small (4/28, 3/24).
- Modes look alike partly because the task and prompt are the same and one human input is light, so the paper does not show that humans add nothing.
- Models used: gpt-5-2025-08-07 and claude-sonnet-4-5-2025-0929. This will date.

BUILDS ON: AlphaEvolve (fixed-objective optimizer, SAGA-Opt is its analog); TextGrad; Biomni, ChemCrow, Coscientist, AI Scientist, AI Co-scientist, Kosmos (Table S1.1); BoltzGen, Germinal, MatterGen, REINVENT4; Göttl et al. (RL flowsheet design); Kahneman "Thinking, Fast and Slow" (inner = fast, outer = slow).

CODE: Scorer interface (Fig 1c, p2): `@scorer(name="morpholine") def score_morpholine(samples: List[str]) -> List[Optional[float]]:`. Scorers are normalized to [0,1], higher is better; filters return 1.0 or 0.0 and are multiplied into the aggregate (p45). Scorers run in Docker over MCP (S1.7).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2). Panel (d) shows co-pilot/semi-pilot/autopilot as which of Planner/Analyzer have a human. Best single figure for note 07.
- Fig 2 (p5). Autopilot feedback demo (2d): Analyzer notices "80% primary amine", Planner adds a scorer.
- Fig 3 (p7). Semi-pilot feedback loop, nanobody.
- Fig 5 (p12) and Fig 6 (p15). Per-mode iteration curves; Fig 6 shows the spread across modes.
- Table S1.1 (p39). Compares AI-scientist systems on human-in-the-loop and self-evolving.

FIT: Best fit is 07-autonomy-ladder as a sharpens/citation with a concrete three-rung gate (which stage the human keeps). It also fits 08-self-improving-loops (the outer loop evolves the scorer, not the agent) and, most strongly, 03-the-scorekeeper: the paper's thesis is that a fixed scorer is gamed, so the scorekeeper must evolve, and the 2-5x fewer oracle calls and p=0.03 composite-score result bear on it. Caution for 07: the paper's rungs are about who edits objectives, not who approves tool calls or starts runs (note 07's four handoffs), so map it as the objective-setting handoff. I would cite it in 07 for the rungs and in 03 for reward hacking and the evolving scorer. I haven't read note 08 closely, so my fit call rests on its headings only.

PROBLEMS: Extraction has no spaces between words (kerned PDF), but all quotes are verbatim from that text. Page numbers are from the in-text page markers. No embedded instructions found. I did not run figures.py. Extracted text is at /tmp/saga.txt.
